text: La Paz literally means “the peace” — named “our lady of the peace” to mark the peace following a civil war

9.	In 1978, this city was one of the very first two places ever inscribed on the brand-new UNESCO World Heritage list (the other was Kraków in Poland). It was founded by the Spanish in 1534 on the ruins of an Inca city, which had itself been built atop a still-older pre-Inca settlement; it nestles right at the foot of the active stratovolcano Pichincha, whose lower slopes loom directly over the city’s western edge. In August 1809, this city was the site of the “Primer Grito de Independencia” — the first cry for independence in all of Spanish America. About 26 km north of the historic center, a yellow-and-red obelisk called the Mitad del Mundo (“Middle of the World”) marks — with a small but well-known eighteenth-century imprecision — the very imaginary line for which the country itself is named. 6.	In the 1990s, authorities in this city installed its first traffic light. Residents complained that it felt cold and impersonal, so they removed it and brought back a white-gloved traffic policeman to manage traffic with graceful, deliberate hand-signals from a small ornate pavilion in the central intersection. Television and the internet were not legalized in this country until 1999, making it the last country in the world to do so. Tashichho Dzong, a fortress-monastery, is the most prominent building that houses both the secretariat of the king’s government and the summer residence of the country’s chief abbot.
